BOOK_A.commentary:
Rule 10.33 was amended in 2020 to add paragraph 2(h), letting the court give effect in costs
to form or to informal offers.
See also the Rules included in Schedule C. Many other general costs topics are discussed in
the notes to R.10.31.
The 2010 Rules do not change the principles of costs, but they do give more detail than the
former Rules did about what factors must be considered.¹
On the interaction of Rr.10.32 and 10.33 factors, see R.10.32n.
A. Costs to Successful Party
1. Limits on Judge's Discretion
See R.10.29 n. A.2
2. Who is Treated as Winner
Usually costs at the end of a suit are awarded and presumed to be properly awarded,²
on the basis of who won the suit on balance, i. e. the nature of the ﬁnal judgment.³
On
misconduct, see Part B below. And costs of an appeal usually go to the winner of the

appeal.¹
Being less successful on appeal than one had been at trial is not a ground to alter the
costs in the trial court.²
Good faith or raising unsettled issues does not shield the loser from costs.³
A plaintiff who succeeds in getting an award of a signiﬁcant amount of damages or debt in her
favor rarely gets as much as she asked for, and often she made some arguments which did not
succeed. That is not ordinarily looked on as divided success, particularly when the unsuccessful
claims or arguments did not much lengthen the suit, and are evidentiary or procedural.⁴
Success
or partial success refers to results, not just to winning one argument; the court does not generally
parse issues for costs purposes.⁵
And several issues with overlapping evidence are not usually
segregated for costs purposes.⁶
It may be different if the ultimate winner litigated issues which
all failed, and raised the winning point only at a late stage, or if the court found the winning point
without counsel’s help.⁷
What is success on an issue is measured objectively.⁸
If there were a number of interlocutory motions, a party may get costs only for the motions
won. If the person losing the suit won one interlocutory motion, whether that decreases the costs
he or she pays one opposite party may depend upon whether various parties were involved and
whether that motion had much to do with this party’s position.⁹

What seems to be a minor issue (e. g. a small counterclaim) which fails, is often ignored for
costs purposes. If the losing party alleges that the minor issue much prolonged the trial, he may
have to prove that through clerks' notes or transcripts.¹
If the main claim and the counterclaim
have essentially the same issues, often no costs are given for the counterclaim, and there is
apportionment of costs, not costs for the counterclaim.²
If the plaintiff wins the main claim and on
the counterclaim, usually the costs are calculated on the amount of the judgment.³
If the costs awarded at trial were too low, the recipient should raise that as a matter of appeal,
not wait and ask for a higher costs level on appeal than the trial level.⁴
Matrimonial litigation follows the usual principles for costs.⁵
It is not true that no one wins a
matrimonial property suit; ordinary principles of costs apply.⁶
But not in insolvency matters?⁷
Where someone has to go to court to get some relief, and the other side shows up but elects
to make no submissions, nor to argue against the application, so that relief is granted, it is proper
to give costs against that respondent to the applicant who got the order.⁸
A respondent to an
application should be ordered to pay costs if the order prayed for is later granted, unless the
respondent plainly states beforehand that he consents, and does not present arguments against
any part of the order later granted.⁹
Half the normal costs were granted where an application
was abandoned, but where it had to be brought and was abandoned simply because after it
was brought the other side gave the relief which had been prayed for.¹⁰
Where an application
was abandoned but it produced some result, namely the concession that a lawyer need not be
called as a witness at trial, and an acknowledgement by one defendant that he had no limitations
defence, cross-costs presumably one-half the normal fee, were allowed.¹¹
If the Court of Appeal reverses the result at trial, the basis for the Trial Judge’s trial costs
decision disappears, and the Court of Appeal can thus revisit trial costs, even if the Trial Judge’s
costs part of his or her decision contained no error.¹²
A contested interlocutory motion for an injunction to obey a contract was granted after a very
late consent, the enjoined party not admitting that he breached the contract, but the applicant
gaining a substantial beneﬁt. The applicant was found partly successful, so it got Schedule C
costs (on column 4).¹³

3. Truly Divided Success
However, where a suit really has several separate parts, or where an unsuccessful argument
has consumed a good deal of the time and money spent in the suit, then the trial judge has the
power to apportion costs because of the divided success.¹
Success is determined objectively from who had the greater success, looking at the outcome,
degree of quantitative and qualitative success, and success on issues or claims. Overall, a
balanced assessment of the outcome and the nature of the ﬁnal judgment is sufﬁcient.²
If each party has some large success, often a trial judge will properly not enter into detailed
calculations, and avoid calculations and set-off, by awarding no costs to either side.³
In true cases of divided success, the judge can either award each side partial costs against
the other (and usually order that they be set off),⁴
or the judge can calculate a rough set-off, and
award reduced costs to one side approximating what the set-off would yield.⁵
Or simply award
no costs, if the offsetting costs would be approximately equal.⁶
or if the exact balance cannot be
exactly calculated.⁷
A party abandoned a key trial issue only after all the evidence at trial had been
heard. Not doing so sooner lengthened the trial. In setting costs, ultimate success is not the only
relevant topic, and success in the other direction on some issues can be looked at. So the plaintiff
should only pay costs for a 4-day trial, not for all 6 days.⁸
There cannot be double counting (double
discount) for lack of full success, e. g. both lower column and fractional costs.⁹
In Alberta, it is traditional to give the plaintiff costs of a size proportional to the net damages
which she recovered, and not to split up costs according to the degrees of blame found at trial.¹⁰
On costs where both the main claim and the counterclaim succeed, see R.3.58 and a review
of the 3 possible results and the 8 topics to weigh.¹¹

4. Excuses to Escape Costs
(a) Irrelevant Poor Excuses
Lack of wrongdoing by the losing party is not a reason to shield him or her from costs.¹
Costs
give a healthy disincentive to bring doubtful claims.²
After all, a lawsuit consumes large resources
owned by both parties and by society. They are gone forever. To award no costs would be a gift to
the losing party and a burden on the winning party.³
A consolation prize is not appropriate.
Costs usually go to the winner, even if the litigation was caused by the tribunal below, not
by the losing party.⁴
But it would be very rare that the tribunal has to pay costs, even on judicial
review.⁵
If judicial review fails because another type of suit is the proper avenue, the government
agency whose decision was not overturned is entitled to costs.⁶
Ease of access to justice is not a ground to refuse to make the losing party pay costs. All
the aims of civil procedure law and the Rules of Court point in the opposite direction. Costs are
designed to promote settlement, deter frivolous actions and defences, deter unnecessary steps,
and sanction those who reject a reasonable settlement offer, as the Supreme Court of Canada
has held. That applies equally to plaintiffs and to defendants.⁷
That one side lacked merit does not prove that the other side had merit.⁸
A limitations statute is not a mere technicality, and serves a beneﬁcial purpose, so failing by
suing too late does not mean that the plaintiff should pay no costs, or only small costs.⁹
The Local Authorities Election Act lets a successful candidate disclaim the seat and be free of
costs. A candidate who supported her election win by opposing a court challenge can be made to
pay costs. The municipality is only liable for costs if the problem was its fault.¹⁰
If a civil suit challenging a Alberta Court of Justice conviction fails, the plaintiff must pay civil
costs, especially if his or her motives are oblique.¹¹
Not seeking costs at stages when a party was unsuccessful is probably not a relevant factor
when the party wins, even as defendant in a class action.¹²
That the case is novel and important to the public, and the losing party stood to make no
money, is not a bar to, nor maybe even a signiﬁcant ground for, exercising to the judge’s discretion
to make him pay costs.¹³

Where a party has a personal interest and stands to gain or lose personally from the suit, and
litigates on the merits but loses, the argument that he or she should pay no costs because the
public has an interest in the outcome, usually lacks any logical foundation.¹
That a costs award would “unduly penalize” the losing party is inaccurate, as costs are primarily
designed for indemnity, not punishment, penalty or beneﬁt.²

(b) Possible Excuses
When and to what level a public authority litigating is subjected to any different costs
considerations is discussed (with analysis of some case law).¹
A party who unnecessarily caused litigation may be denied costs.²
But in a class action, “public interest” includes issues of broad public importance or persons
historically disadvantaged in society, such as those elderly and disabled.³
Other irrelevant excuses which do not shield a litigant from paying costs include impecuniosity,⁴
having followed legal advice and being ignorant of the laws,⁵
that no money was sought in this
lawsuit,⁶
or what the winner will or will not spend the costs on.⁷
B. Costs for Misconduct⁸
1. Introduction
On full-indemnity (solicitor-client) costs for litigation misconduct, see R.10.31 n. I.
Misconduct, even what is not truly egregious, by one party in inducing⁹
or prosecuting or

defending the suit, is a frequently-used ground for denying costs to that party though it won,¹
or
for increasing the costs which that party would otherwise pay.²
Indeed misconduct and difﬁcult
behavior may demand enhanced costs, and allow the Court of Appeal to intervene if they are not
given.³
Increased costs for misconduct are especially ﬁt if the resulting expense to the opponent
was predictable, and the volume of materials before the court was large.⁴
This use of costs is now
more important, given R.1.2 and the emphasis on proportionality and economy, the need for court
sanctions for misconduct short of contempt, and the need for court supervision.⁵
Sometimes the higher costs for misconduct are to punish the wrongdoer, but often they are
proper compensation for the innocent party.⁶
Of course punishing includes deterring misconduct.
"Punitive costs" are not a third category separate from party-party and solicitor-client costs.
Indemnity is the primary principle underpinning cost.⁷
That there is no contempt of court is no bar to assessing extra costs for misconduct.⁸
Indeed
if a motion for contempt fails, the party accused of contempt may have to pay elevated costs for
his misconduct.⁹
Litigation misconduct can take many forms. But mere lack of merit in the suit, even misconceived
litigation, is not misconduct,¹⁰
unless the position was patently indefensible, having almost no
chance of succeeding, frivolous or vexatious.¹¹
Usually the costs penalty for misconduct is conﬁned to the expense or inconvenience of that
particular misconduct, or of correcting it; changing the cost of the whole suit requires systemic and
persistent misconduct.¹²
If one party is guilty of bad enough misconduct for full-indemnity costs but
the other side needlessly lengthened the litigation somewhat, the otherwise-suitable full indemnity
ﬁgure may be reduced somewhat.¹³

These principles of higher costs for misconduct apply also in child-custody cases,¹
and in
estate litigation.²
One must not conﬂate punitive damages and punitive costs, which differ fundamentally; usually
the former is for pre-suit misconduct and the latter for post-suit.³
Punitive damage awards are not
an automatic bar to higher (or full-indemnity) costs for litigation misconduct.⁴
But clear evidence and advance notice of the allegation and the costs issue are needed.⁵
Sometimes, misconduct on both sides may cancel out.⁶
One element supporting increased costs payable for litigation misconduct can be the fact that
the innocent party’s counsel charged an unsually low hourly rate.⁷
A party faced with an accusation of misconduct being used to seek special costs, should
either give his explanation to the ﬁrst judicial ofﬁcer (e. g. an Applications Judge ruling on costs), or
should at least say that there was a matter before the Law Society, and that he was not at liberty
to disclose the facts then. He cannot remain silent and then later raise this defence.⁸
2. Examples of Occasions for Higher Costs⁹
Sometimes misconduct removes the right to get costs, e. g. where the guilty party wins. Those
examples are included in this Part B.2.
Examples¹⁰
of such misconduct allowing higher costs or extra costs, are dishonesty; perjur y or fraud;¹¹

fraud or crime¹
(whether as a sword or a shield) ;²
forging medical certiﬁcates;³
breach of the Rules;⁴
improperly withholding papers or information⁵
(e. g. , during discovery,⁶
or during requests for

disclosure,¹
or in response to a request for papers referred to in an expert report²
); delay;³
repeated
non-appearances causing an opponent to travel unnecessarily;⁴
contempt;⁵
breach of orders;⁶

intemperate and unnecessarily inﬂammatory submissions;¹
unfounded allegations of conspiracy
or fraud;²
conﬂict; bad faith; unfounded allegations of racism against counsel;³
exaggerated
claims;⁴
continuing complex, expensive suit while possessing papers showing the suit was brought
too late;⁵
forcing the opponent to prove facts not seriously in doubt;⁶
inaccurately recounting the
afﬁdavit evidence to a chambers judge;⁷
alleging a nonexistent emergency;⁸
introducing a host
of irrelevant oral and documentary evidence thus much lengthening the trial;⁹
leaving to trial two
interlocutory applications which should have been disposed of before;¹⁰
sloppily providing an out-
of-date copy of one’s own key by-law;¹¹
moving for a rehearing of the whole appeal, on slender
grounds;¹²
raising a new point or a conﬂict late, thus compelling an adjournment;¹³
changing one's

evidence between examination for discovery and trial, so surprising the opponent;¹
failing to
disclose important facts during an application;²
deliberately understating the time needed for
trial, to avoid need for a pretrial conference;³
reneging on a deal with the other side, after taking
its beneﬁts;⁴
failing to approve a draft order and later trying to rely on its non-entry;⁵
general
prolixity and over-litigation;⁶
vexatious relitigation;⁷
not citing authorities to the court;⁸
a solicitor
not making her retainer known, so there could be no pre-trial cooperation;⁹
various steps by a
solvent debtor to frustrate enforcement of the judgment;¹⁰
an intervener arguing issues on which
no leave to argue had been granted;¹¹
a false certiﬁcate that all experts’ reports have been served;¹²
champerty;¹³
keeping a lis pendens on land not subject to the suit;¹⁴
carrying on under a permit
despite a statutory stay pending appeal;¹⁵
disallowing votes on grounds very technical or picky,
mistaken, or because of clerical errors by the same party disallowing;¹⁶
stalling his own lawsuit and
evading all his duties as a plaintiff;¹⁷
commencing and stalling a lawsuit with excessive claims never
intended to proceed to a result, and just brought as a bargaining chip to cost the opponent money;¹⁸
obsessiveness and reluctance to accept court rulings;¹⁹
levying execution (enforcement) which
has no legal basis;²⁰
refusing reasonable requests for a stay of enforcement;²¹
very persistently

interfering with opposing counsel’s cross-examination on afﬁdavit, by interrupting, answering for
the witness, coaching the witness, or reframing the question, though carefully warned, with case
law;¹
continuing until a very late stage (after all cross-examination and argument) to insist on
sloppy incorrect information on an important point, despite early explanation and demonstration,
under oath, by the opponent of the inaccuracy;²
refusing to participate in dispute resolution;³
notarizing pseudolegal papers;⁴
disclosing very bulky ﬁnancial information long outstanding only
a week before the scheduled hearing.⁵
Even if discovery or disclosure is not refused or is not falsely claimed complete, very lengthy
delay in giving or completing discovery or disclosure, with no good explanation, is also litigation
conduct founding costs penalties or enhancement or denial.⁶
For years costs for failure to admit what a notice to admit called for was dealt with in a separate
Rule, but since 2010, R.10.33(2) (b) has given the costs penalty, which courts should not hesitate
to apply, without ﬁnding excuse for the non-admission.⁷
A new allegation of fraudulent concealment to bypass a limitations defence ﬁrst raised on
appeal, seems to have been a ground to raise costs from the 1½ x column 5 at trial, to double
column 5 on appeal.⁸
Where each side claimed that the other was guilty of litigation misconduct (largely in the trial
court) and both parties were very aggressive and made strong accusations and thus made the
litigation more complex, that was an additional reason for trebling column C, but not for any further
costs adjustment.⁹
One reason for no costs was failure to ﬁle a quantiﬁcation of the costs ordered by the trial
judge, as the Court asked before hearing of the application in question.¹⁰
Having no lawyer is no excuse for litigation misconduct, especially repeated misconduct.¹¹
Whether to increase costs for misconduct is owed deference on appeal.¹²
One of the principal aims of the Rules of Court is to prevent multiplicity of proceedings.
Therefore, where two proceedings are conducted where one would do, or some steps are
unnecessary,¹³
costs may be used as a remedy.

The Surrogate Rules give additional grounds for extra costs for misconduct.¹
Demanding
formal proof of a will in a trial is misconduct where if the will were invalid, that would have no
effect, as the will gave exactly the same result as would an intestacy.²
3. Examples of Usual Standard of Costs
But changing a company’s constitution and so beneﬁtting oneself is not such misconduct as
warrants higher costs, if the change was made long before suit was brought, and ﬁling with the
government had been simply neglected.³
The fact that a trial judge preferred the evidence of one party over the other’s, does not
necessarily mean that the latter gave false evidence, nor tried to deceive the court.⁴
Conversely,
no rule bars enhanced costs for litigation misconduct based on credibility ﬁndings, especially if it
is of an unusual and high degree, beyond the trial judge’s simply accepting the evidence of one
witness over others.⁵
Accusations of misconduct will affect the costs only if the misconduct is in the litigation, and
the accusations are proved or readily ascertainable.⁶
And a mere passing reference in evidence to
fraud, not pursued or argued, is not a ground to increase (or alter) costs.⁷
Allegations of fraud or
the like, not scandalous in wording, and whose substance the court had not yet ruled on, did not
justify full indemnity costs.⁸
Mild slackness or poor drafting was not bad enough to increase costs.⁹
Merely losing a lawsuit does not constitute misconduct,¹⁰
but later in the lawsuit the strong
probability of losing one or more issues, especially in a case not very complex, may be evidence
of substantive unreasonableness, and doubly so if very large sums are claimed, especially in light
of R.10.33(2) on denial or refusal to admit.¹¹

When setting costs in a family or divorce matter, after a trial, the court should not look into
whether there was misconduct when an earlier Emergency Protection Order was obtained, as
no “chill” on such proceedings should be imposed, especially if it was some years before and
memories are no longer fresh.¹
Here are a number of examples of behavior which is not misconduct. Asserting a wrong
interpretation of a contract.²
An unproven plea of conspiracy if conduct of the defendant at ﬁrst
made conspiracy seem likely.³
Refusal to agree to judicial dispute resolution.⁴
Not giving ongoing
oral discovery, and not warning before trial that one’s evidence would change.⁵
Not forcing the
other side to prove a fact not originally in issue, not prolonging the trial, nor creating other delays,
nor concealing material evidence, nor failing to produce things in a timely manner, without deceit,
intimidation, nor misrepresentation.⁶
Litigating over whether a plan of arrangement extinguished
a claim.⁷
Misguided motions and irrelevant cross-examination and irrelevant submissions.⁸
A late
failed request for a third party notice.⁹
That a motion should have gone to an afternoon special,
even if the judge also had concerns about that, where neither party suggested that, and instead
both were willing to argue the application on the merits then.¹⁰
Beating the opponent's offer by only a slight amount does not affect costs, except in exceptional
circumstances.¹¹
4. Amount of Costs for Misconduct
Such higher costs should at least be enough to indemnify fully the innocent party’s expenses
directly caused by the wrongdoing; and they may be more, intended to denounce or punish the
wrongdoer. In one case it was the full lawyer’s bill for time in court, and half his bill for preparation.¹²
Since the misconduct does not typically operate throughout the lawsuit, often it leads to a lump-
sum increase in the costs otherwise payable, but not to full indemnity costs for the whole suit.¹³
There should not be a reward of costs plus something else.¹⁴
Even if it is proper to order full indemnity costs, some adjustments to the legal bill incurred by
the innocent and winning party may be needed, and how to verify the bills’ overall reasonableness
may involve more time and effort than it is worth. Where the bills were very lengthy and detailed
and stretched over about 6 1/2 years, and the losing party did not question those accounts, and

the (self-represented) losing party’s legal work was thousands of hours and several times the
hours incurred by the lawyers for the winning innocent party, and where the losing party had
always been uncooperative and hard to deal with, and so examining anyone’s legal bills would
not be quick or easy, the court did not check the winner’s legal bills in detail. Instead the judge
calculated the proper column of Schedule C, and instead chose a multiple of the proper column
of Schedule C. The court chose a multiplier which would produce about the same as the amount
of full-indemnity expenses claimed by the winner as costs (except for a smaller multiplier for one
issue). So the court awarded a lump-sum as costs (plus disbursements), hinting that that would
come to a multiplier of Schedule C of 3 or 4 times.¹
It is common to deny a winner part of his costs where his counsel wasted time at trial with
irrelevancies.²
Despite divided success, an offending party had to pay full Schedule C costs
plus an extra $2, 500.³
For contemptuous refusal to produce documents, the Schedule C costs
(already large) were doubled.⁴
For costs and denial of permission to bring applications, because
of contempt, see R.10.53 nn. C, D. Similarly for delaying and obstructing setting down for trial.⁵
On thrown-away costs, see R.10.31, n. C(g).
If grave misconduct was alleged without proof during an interlocutory proceeding, and the
suit is ongoing, the chambers judge can award lump-sum enhanced costs for that, with leave to
renew the topic before the trial judge at the end of the suit and then seek more money to bring
the interlocutory costs up to full indemnity.⁶
Three quarters of full indemnity was awarded for a
cluster of unethical behaviors.⁷
Or 80% of full indemnity.⁸
Or (coupled with not accepting offers)
full indemnity.⁹
A judge cannot change an earlier judge's costs order, nor give more penalties for alleged
misconduct already ruled on by an earlier judge.¹⁰
5. Failure to Admit
An important but often overlooked Rule is R.10.33(2) (b). Defendants very often deny
everything, and make the plaintiff prove what the defendant knows is clearly true. The Rule
authorizes a special costs award in such cases.¹¹
Even if the pleadings are ﬁne on their face, and
even if there was no notice to admit under R.6.37, at the end of trial a losing party can ask for
costs of part of the trial when the opposing party has denied things which turn out to have been
plainly correct and should have been admitted.¹²

For example, often a plaintiff sues for goods or services sold and delivered, but the defendant
proves at trial that they were faulty and so the amount owing is greatly reduced or even eliminated.
Usually the defendant has denied the contract and delivery of the goods in his pleadings, and
made the plaintiff prove that. The plaintiff should cite R.10.33(2) (b) and get costs of proving the
contract and delivery.¹
It is proper to penalize a defendant’s refusal to admit a very plain case,²
even if the defendant is represented by an insurer.³
A liability insurer will often maintain a denial
of liability up to trial, when liability is very clear, and only quantum is in issue, and that should be
more frequently penalized in costs.
6. Expenses Caused Without Fault
A party may have to pay costs of adjournments which it caused, even if no one was at fault.⁴
Despite R.10.33(2) (c), two sets of costs were appropriate, though both proceedings had the
same aim (spare an afﬁant cross-examination), because they were by two separate law ﬁrms and
on somewhat different issues.⁵
7. Who Pays Costs Penalty
Rule 10.49 expressly lets the court order one of the lawyers to pay costs personally.⁶
And the
common law gives the court a broad power to order anyone to pay costs, even though he or she
is not a party to the suit.⁷
That may be done:
(a) where that non-party is the person ultimately liable⁸
(e. g. on a chain of contracts), or
(b) where he or she was the real instigator of the litigation and the one which would have
received the fruits,⁹
(c) where the named parties were ﬁctitious;¹⁰
or
(d) where the non-party was guilty of serious misconduct relating to the suit.¹¹

Courts have approved items (a) to (c), but point out that they are not an exhaustive list.¹
Costs against a lawyer personally, at the end of a suit, are unusual, and not a topic with
wide discretion. Serious misconduct or seriously undermining the court’s authority or serious
interference with the administration of justice, is needed. Unfounded frivolous or vexatious
proceedings have to denote a serious abuse. A mere error is not enough, unless there is gross
neglect or inaccuracy, or a marked and unacceptable departure from the standard or reasonable
conduct for a lawyer.²
Before such a ﬁnding and award, there must of course be notice to the non-party, and a
chance to argue against his or her liability.³
Seventy-ﬁve percent of the costs awarded to one winning party and 25% of the costs to
another winning party were to be jointly and severally payable by the losing party’s counsel. That
is exceptional, but there was serious misconduct. Counsel had lots of notice, by correspondence
and then a written brief for costs, almost 2 years before. And these lawyers had seen that the
misconduct complained of was theirs.⁴
A non-proﬁt body which voluntarily took over litigation which a private person had abandoned,
the body wishing the court to set some rule of law, but lost, had to pay almost full indemnity costs.⁵

commentary.text: Rule 10.33 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.33. 1. Evidence in Costs Applications In Mitran v. Guarantee RV Centre Inc. (1999), 72 Alta. L.R. (3d) 54 (Q.B.), counsel made submissions to the court as the “reasonableness” of certain costs being sought. In the course of those submissions he made certain assertions of fact not found in the evidence. In determining that those assertions by counsel could not be considered as evidence, Johnstone J. held, at p. 62, that “the evidence available on the costs application is restricted to sworn evidence” because “any submissions he made were merely hearsay.” 2. “Reasonableness” When considering the reasonableness or otherwise of an expenditure made by the defendant I must view the matter through the eyes of the defendant and in light of the problem facing it when the expenditure was made. The test of reasonableness is not, in my opinion, entirely based on the importance of the expenditure to success at trial. Hindsight may show that some liabilities assumed were, in the end, of little or no benefit. The question is whether the expense was reasonable and proper in the light of the circumstances which existed at the time it was incurred. The issues raised from time to time by the pleadings and by discovery and production are significant circumstances. The magnitude of the expenditure in relation to the amount at risk in the proceedings is another important consideration. In all cases the party taxing costs has the burden of showing that both the nature of the expense and its amount were reasonable and proper in the circumstances. Petrogas Processing Ltd. v. Westcoast Transmission Co. (1990), 105 A.R. 384 (Q.B.), at 394, per O'Leary J. Madam Justice Johnstone in MacCabe v. Westlock Roman Catholic Separate School District No. 110 (1999), 70 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1 (Q.B.); additional reasons at (1999) 73 Alta. L.R. (3d) 107 (Q.B.), at pp. 22–23, set forth the following factors to consider when assessing the reasonableness of a claimed disbursement: It is clear that an award for disbursements is within my discretion. In determining whether or not a disbursement is reasonable, I may consider the following factors: (a) the length of the trial; (b) its complexity; (c) the nature and number of the issues involved in the trial; (d) the degree of contest as to evidentiary matters; (e) the degree of contest as to credibility of witnesses, including professional expert witnesses; (f) the nature and number of the defenses mounted; (g) the requirement for and use of experts; (h) the use of models, tests and scientific evidence; (i) the nature and amount of damages at issue; (j) the relationship of the expeses claimed as costs to the amounts at issue in damages; (k) any agreement of counsel to share specific expense items. Her Ladyship then quoted with approval O'Leary J.'s statement in Petrogas Processing Ltd. v. Westcoast Transmission Co. (1990), 105 A.R. 384 (Q.B.) (reproduced above). She said that “the overriding consideration therefore is the reasonableness of the disbursement in light of the circumstances which existed at the time it was incurred” (p. 23). At p. 30 she relied on the following statement of Leggat J. in Morrissette v. Smith (1990), 39 C.P.C. (2d) 30 (B.C. S.C.): [the] Test was whether, at the time the expense was incurred, it was a proper disbursement in the sense of not being extravagant, negligent, mistaken or the result of excessive caution or excessive zeal, judged by the situation at the time when the expense was incurred. 3. Unnecessary litigation For a list of actions which have been found to constitute “unnecessary litigation”[Rule 10.33(2)d)], please see Condominium Corporation No 022 5899 v. 499430 Alberta Ltd, 2020 ABQB 233, 2020 CarswellAlta 625 at paragraphs 59–61. 4. Discretion with Respect to Costs In Chisholm v. Lindsay, 2015 ABCA 179, the Court said: 44 As we see it, the purpose of the Rules of Court is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly, justly and expeditiously resolved either by a Court process in a timely and cost-effective way or in some other fashion, as the Rules contemplate. In every case, the relevant inquiry will be whether there was a legitimate attempt to settle given the issues in dispute and mindful of the conduct of the litigation. Such an approach encourages settlements without derogating from that referred to as the foundation of the formal Rules. Maheasserts that notwithstanding strict compliance with the formal Rules of Court, a trial judge must be permitted to take account, in the context of other factors, of non-compliant offers made in good faith to settle litigation. The first matter is to consider the Court's discretionary rights … the Court has a wide area of discretion in awarding costs under R. 601 of the Alberta Rules of Court. See also s. 19 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. C-29. Although the Court's discretion in ordering costs is traditionally very wide, it is not a discretion without bounds with the scope of such discretion being recently discussed by Mason J. in Pharand Ski Corp. v. Alberta (1991), [81 Alta. L.R. (2d) 304] (Q.B.), at p. 398: While the court has a wide discretion when awarding costs, the discretion must be exercised judicially and in accordance with established principles. This broad discretion comes from, and is based upon the absolute discretion vested in the Court of Chancery in England with respect to costs. As such, it is to be exercised in accordance with the precepts and historical precedents established by that court and developed therefrom, by case law based upon a proper application and extension of those precedents. See Andrews v. Barnes (1887), 39 Ch. D. 133 and Mobil Oil of Canada Limited v. Canadian Superior Oil Limited and Neilsen, supra. Claudio's Restaurant Group Inc. v. Calgary (City) (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 141 (Q.B.), at 147–48, per Rooke J. In Papaschase Indian Band No. 136 v. Canada (Attorney General) (2004), 45 Alta. L.R. (4th) 72 (Q.B.), Slatter J. reviewed the discretion which may be exercised in matters of costs. At p. 79, his Lordship said: The Court of Appeal in [Pauli v. ACE INA Insurance (2005), 1 W.W.R. 12 (Alta. C.A.)] recognized the usual rule that costs follow the event. However, the Court held that this normal rule can be displaced when some or all of the following factors are present: (a) the decision resolves a new or unsettled point, and it was in the public interest that the point be settled. In such cases it is relevant whether the litigants have a direct pecuniary interest in the proceedings, and whether the issue extends beyond the immediate interests of the parties. While the Court recognized that all decisions have some precedential value, and that that did not mean that all litigation was in the public interest, it concluded that settling the point in the Pauli action was of public interest. (b) Costs may not follow the event if a novel point is involved. The Court held that the interpretation of the standard form of insurance contract at issue in Pauli raised a novel point. (c) The Court also concluded that Pauli was a test case, which is another reason to depart from the normal costs rule. While the class in Pauli was defined so widely that it would cover every person in Alberta with a similar claim, the Court held that the decision might prove persuasive in other similar actions. Garneau Lofts Inc. (2005), 59 Alta. L.R. (4th) 255 (Q.B.), Slatter J. (as he then was), at pp. 258–264, gave the following summary of the concept of “thrown away costs”: The concept of “thrown away costs” arises because in Alberta our system of civil procedure is largely “prejudice-based”. A failure to comply with the Rules will generally not be fatal so long as any prejudice to the other side can be remedied by an award of costs, an adjournment, or some other type of relief. This general rule has many manifestations, but some of the more specific ones are: (a) a missed deadline in the Rules will not be fatal if any prejudice can be remedied by costs. (b) if a judgment is entered or a step is taken in default of appearance of one of the parties, the step taken in default can often be opened up. (c) if a pleading is for some reason deficient or inadequate, an amendment will generally be allowed, so long as there is no prejudice that cannot be remedied. (d) late applications for adjournments of scheduled court appearances will often be granted, again so long as any prejudice can be remedied in some way. This prejudice-based system of proceedings has been criticized on the basis that it is too unstructured, and it leads to delay and added expense. Nevertheless, it remains the general rule governing civil practice in Alberta. Apart from the general principle that procedural missteps that can be remedied will not be fatal, there are some specific rules relating to particular types of missteps. Without attempting to state in detail the law or the tests applicable, some examples include: (a) there are some specific Rules, such as Rules 190 and 538(4), which deal with the consequences of missing specific time requirements in the Rules. (b) in opening up a noting in default, the moving party must generally provide some explanation for non-appearance, must show that the application to open up was brought promptly, and must demonstrate a triable defence. (c) as a general rule, Rule 141 provides that an amending party is not entitled to costs of the amendment of a pleading. (This Rule is perhaps somewhat academic given the repeal of the specific item in Schedule “C” that used to allow a separate fee for amendment of pleadings.) (d) where a late adjournment is granted, costs will often be awarded for wasted preparation, keeping in mind that not all preparation will be completely lost. In any of these situations, “thrown away costs” may be awarded as a method of negating any prejudice that might otherwise fall on the responding party. What costs are “thrown away” will depend on the particular type of application being brought, and the cases must be examined to see the particular context in which they were decided.8 In dealing with what are truly “thrown away costs”, all of these procedural situations break down into two parts: (a) there is initially some procedural misstep by the applicant party, be that the faulty drafting of a pleading, the failure to attend in court on the appropriate date, the failure to be ready to proceed on a scheduled trial date, or the missing of a deadline. This procedural misstep causes the responding party to take some step (such as getting a default judgment, preparing for a trial that is adjourned, or responding to the faulty pleading), or perhaps it may simply cause delay and require an application to comply with the Rules (in the case of a missed deadline). When the applicant later tries to correct its misstep, the action taken by the respondent becomes “wasted” or “thrown away”. (b) the second step is then to resolve whether the applicant who made the misstep is entitled to some relief. At this stage of the proceedings, the applicant who committed the procedural misstep alleges that he or she is within the general rule that missteps are allowed so long as there is no prejudice that is not remediable in some way. The respondent might concede that the applicant has met the test, or may assert that the applicant is not entitled to relief, and resist the application. There may then be a contested proceeding over whether the applicant is entitled to relief. … Thrown Away Costs There is conflicting case law on the concept of thrown away costs. There are two competing philosophies. The first is that the applicant who made the misstep is seeking an indulgence, and must pay all the costs of seeking the indulgence, even if it is clear on the authorities that the applicant is entitled to the indulgence: Fox v. Bourget (1987), 17 C.P.C. (2d) 94 (Ont. Dist. Ct.) citing Aliferis v. Parfeniuk (1985), 1 C.P.C. (2d) 41, 9 O.A.C. 215 (Ont. C.A.), although Aliferis does not appear to state any general principle to that effect. In the leading case of Burgoine v. Taylor (1878), 9 Ch. D. 1 (Eng. Ch. Div.) a judgment was entered in default of appearance due to an error by a solicitor. The Defendant was initially unsuccessful in opening up the judgment, but succeeded on appeal, where Jessel, M.R. said: Solicitors cannot, any more than other men, conduct their business without sometimes making slips; and where a solicitor watches the list, and happens to miss the case, in consequence of which it is taken in his absence, it is in accordance with justice and with the course of practice to restore the action to the paper, on the terms of the party in default paying the costs of the day, which include all costs thrown away by reason of the trial becoming abortive. As a general rule, solicitors in my branch of the Court consent to such an order as is now asked, and that such an application should be opposed is to me a novelty. Still, as the Appellant was in default, he must pay the costs of the application to the Court below, but no costs of the appeal. Thus, the applicant had to pay costs, even though he was successful, and entitled to the relief according to the practice of the Court. Other cases have followed a more functional approach, under which only the costs that are truly wasted are payable. Smith v. Harrington (1994), 36 C.P.C. (3d) 209 (Ont. Gen. Div.) followed this approach, citing Royal Bank v. Blatt (1991), 26 A.C.W.S. (3d) 926 (Ont. Gen. Div.): An award of costs thrown away is to compensate the party for the work done in preparing for a trial that did not occur. I agree with the following statement adopted by Assessment Officer Conover in Nippa v. C.H. Lewis (Lucan Ltd.), January 28, 1988, unreported, that: …costs thrown away on a solicitor and client scale is intended to result in full indemnity for all steps which were reasonably necessary to proceed with the action but which have been rendered useless by the other party's conduct in responding or not responding to the action. This approach has the advantage of discouraging the respondent from opposing relief that the applicant is entitled to, because the respondent will get costs of the motion even if unsuccessful, as happened in Burgoine v. Taylor. The dispute, at its root, is whether the rule that the successful party is prima facie entitled to costs applies. On the one hand, if the applicant asserts a right to fix an error, and wins in the face of resistence to that relief, the applicant should get costs. On the other hand, it is asserted that the party who made the error should pay, because it caused the problem and is seeking an indulgence. … The Court of Queen's Bench Costs Manual, prepared by the Taxing Officers, defines “thrown away costs” as follows: “Thrown Away Costs” Are those that a party would not have incurred save for the actions of another party. The most common would be the costs awarded a Plaintiff upon the successful setting aside of his/her default judgment. Consider the following: Item # Description Thrown Away Cost? 1 Pleadings (drafting, filing & serving Statement of Claim) no 6(2) Ex Parte Application for a Substitutional Service Order no 1 Noting in Default (a component of Item 1—get a proportion yes of the Item) 2 Uncontested Assessment Application yes 5 Examination on Affidavit re: application to set aside default yes judgment 7(1) Defence of Application to Set Aside Default Judgment yes The Manual treats as thrown away not only the wasted effort of the respondent, but also the steps taken by the applicant to determine if it has a right to correct the original error.18 The general pattern in these cases is that when a party makes a procedural misstep, that party will then assert to the respondent that it has the right to correct that misstep if it eliminates all the prejudice. For example, it may assert that it has the right to amend a defective pleading, on payment of the costs of any wasted effort by the respondent. It might assert a right to open up a noting in default, because it has met the legal test for doing that (supra, para. 7(b)), again on payment of wasted costs. The respondent can do one of two things: it can acknowledge that the applicant has the right to fix the misstep, because the applicable test has been met, including that any prejudice can be eliminated on appropriate terms, or it can deny that the applicant has the right to correct the misstep. In the latter situation, a new sub-dispute is created. There is now an issue as to whether the appropriate test (e.g. to amend, to adjourn, to open up noting in default, etc.) has been met. When this issue is litigated, the general rule should be that costs follow the event, subject of course to the Court's general jurisdiction over costs. Granting costs to an unsuccessful party only encourages unreasonable opposition to relief to which the applicant is entitled. Therefore, as a general rule where (for example) one party asserts a right to amend pleadings, and the other party denies that right, and the amending party must take the matter to court, costs should follow the event. If the applicant succeeds in its motion to amend, it should get costs. Rule 141 says simply that the amending party must bear the costs of the amendment (as I have previously mentioned, supra, para. 7(c), a reference to a now repealed part of Schedule “C”). Rule 141 does not say that the applicant must pay the costs of the fight over whether it has the right to amend, even if it wins that fight. That would be a most undesirable result, because it would mean that the respondents on motions like that could defend them with impunity, knowing that win or lose they would receive costs. Absent some positive misconduct, the successful moving party should get costs of the motion to permit the amendment. Likewise, if a party is noted in default, but asserts that it has met the test for opening up a default, it should be entitled to costs if successful. If the respondent denies that the defaulting party has the right to open up the default, and forces the matter to Chambers, then costs should follow the event. Again, it would be an undesirable result to allow respondents to defend such applications regardless of the merits of the applicant's position. The applicant may have caused the noting in default, but it did not cause the subsequent court battle about whether it was entitled to open up the noting in default. With applications to adjourn, a distinction should be drawn between the effort that will be wasted if there is an adjournment, and the dispute over the right to an adjournment. In principle, if the applicant asserts a right to adjournment, and under the prevailing rules and practice the applicant is entitled to that adjournment, then if the respondent resists, costs should follow the event. However, if the adjournment is the result of some fault of the applicant, the applicant is often required to pay the costs of the adjournment application, even if successful. This is an exception to Rule 607. It should be noted that in these situations the costs of determining whether the applicant is entitled to be relieved of its procedural misstep is not really “wasted”. There is a dispute over the rights of the applicant to relief from its error, and the application resolves that dispute. Those efforts are not “wasted”, because the dispute must be resolved. Furthermore, those proceedings are not a direct result of the procedural misstep of the applicant; they are really brought on by the respondent's failure to accept that the applicant has made out its right to be relieved of the consequence of its procedural misstep. Where the applicant is entitled to relief the respondent should not unreasonably litigate the point. As a result, the rule that costs go to the successful party (Rule 607) should prevail over any rule about “wasted” costs. In summary, a distinction should be drawn between: (a) the costs of the wasted work caused by the procedural misstep that is the source of the problem, and (b) litigating the dispute over whether the person who took the misstep has the right to fix it. The principle that the Rules are prejudice-based, and that procedural errors should be forgiven if prejudice can be eliminated, must be balanced against the other rule that costs generally go to the successful party: Rule 607. Subject to the overriding discretion of the judge over costs, only the first category of costs (paragraph (a)) are “thrown away”. 15. Purpose of Costs I am aware that the principle and purpose behind the wording of party-and-party costs is to provide indemnity to the person entitled to them Such Rules of Court are not designed for the purpose of punishing, penalizing or benefitting a party to an action. In Alberta, except in unique circumstances, party-and-party costs will not approach indemnification of the successful party and thus it is more accurate to describe the awarding of costs as a contribution toward the successful party's expense in prosecuting or defending the action. Wenden v. Trikha (1992), 1 Alta L.R. (3d) 283 (Q.B.), at 293, per Murray J. And McDonald J. said: While the allocation of costs of a lawsuit is always in the discretion of the court, the exercise of that discretion must be consistent with established principles and practice. It is traditionally accepted in Canada's common law provinces that as a general rule the successful party recovers its costs from the unsuccessful party. However, such recovery is normally on a party-and-party basis. That is, the costs recoverable are those fees fixed for the steps in the proceeding by a schedule of fees (Sched. C. in Alberta's Rules of Court), plus reasonable disbursements. It is not intended that the successful party receive full indemnification of those fees and disbursements which it would be charged by its counsel. In England the degree of indemnification appears to be considerably higher than is normal in Canada. In almost all jurisdictions of the United States of America the rule is that no costs are recoverable by the successful party. The Canadian practice reflects an attempt to balance two conflicting interests. On the one hand, it is argued that if a party is successful and there are no circumstances constituting blameworthiness in the conduct of the litigation by that party, it is unfair to require the successful party to bear any costs incurred by his counsel in prosecuting or defending the action. On the other hand, it is argued that if the unsuccessful party is required to bear all the costs of the successful party, citizens will be unduly hesitant to sue to assert their rights (even valid ones) or to defend their rights when sued. The partial indemnity practice as it exists in Canada is a compromise intended to give some scope in practice for each of the conflicting policy considerations. When the case is of considerable magnitude and complexity, the practice in Alberta contemplates that the court may order the unsuccessful party to pay a multiple of the fees that are fixed by Sched. C. But even then it is not intended that there be full indemnity, except in extraordinary circumstances. Reese v. Alberta (1993), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40 (Q.B.), at 44–45, per McDonald J. 16. Consider Complexity and Difficulty of Proceedings In addition to s. 19 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act and the relevant Rules of Court, McCarthy v. Bd. of Trustees, supra, is authority for the proposition that the difficulty and complexity of the proceedings are relevant in considering the scale of party-party costs to be awarded. Similarly, in the Alberta Court of Appeal case of Calbar Securities Ltd. v. Toole Peet Co. (1984), 30 Alta. L.R. (2d) 286 … which upheld the trial judge's award of costs on triple col. 5 with no limiting rule to apply, the late McGillivray C.J.A. held at pp. 287–88: The court is of the opinion that the scale of costs and the exclusion of the limiting rule cannot be based on the number of parties who are to pay the costs, but should depend upon the amount involved, the complexity and importance of the issues, and the length of trial. In New Brunswick, the Court of Appeal in Williams v. New Brunswick; St. John v. Williams; Chubb Indust. Ltd. v. St. John (1985), 34 C.C.L.T. 299 at 320 … held that, although the amount recovered in a lawsuit has always been important, it … is not the sole criterion and in fixing costs the Court may consider other matters including the complexity of the proceedings, the importance of the issues, the conduct of the parties, the manner in which the proceedings were conducted and any other matter relevant to the question of costs. Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1987), 50 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 (Q.B.), at 10–11, per Wachowich J. 17. When punitive damages have been awarded In Indutech Canada Ltd. v. Gibbs Pipe Distributors Ltd., 2012 ABQB 425, 2012 CarswellAlta 1909, 84 Alta. L.R. (5th) 55, the successful Plaintiffs sought enhanced costs. The defendants submitted that since punitive damages had been awarded against them, costs should not be enhanced. Madam Justice Romaine disagreed, and, at paragraphs 11–12, said: 11 The Gibbs Group Defendants submit that where a party has been punished for misconduct by an award of punitive damages, as was the case here, courts have been disinclined to punish that party further through a costs award: 539618 Ontario Ltd. v. Stathopoulos (1989), 17 A.C.W.S. (3d) 159 (Ont.H.C.J.) at para. 8. 12 It may be more accurate to say that an award of punitive damages may be a factor in considering enhanced costs, since the rules and case authority in Alberta do not preclude the consideration of misconduct at the costs stage of proceedings, whether or not punitive damages have been found to be appropriate. Punitive damages reflect the misconduct of the Gibbs Group Defendants over the course of the Agency Agreement. An enhanced costs award reflects misconduct during the course of the litigation, and there is evidence of such misconduct in the findings of credibility made with respect to various of the Gibbs Group Defendants. Justice Romaine's decision was unsuccessfully appealed (Indutech Canada Ltd. v. Gibbs Pipe Distributors Ltd., 2013 ABCA 111, 2013 CarswellAlta 957, 544 A.R. 205, 82 Alta. L.R. (5th) 217). The Court said, at paragraphs 100, and 102–106: 100 In a companion appeal, the appellants appeal the trial judge's awarded enhanced costs under some categories available under Column 5 of Schedule C of the Rules of Court. They do not contest the award of enhanced costs in relation to other categories. Her award elevated the costs payable by the appellants above the $285,000 which would have otherwise been ordered paid by them. … 102 She rejected the argument that enhanced costs should not be awarded because the harm they addressed was met by the award of punitive damages. Her award was grounded in the nature of the litigation itself. She accepted that an award of punitive damages should reflect misconduct prior to the commencement of the litigation and of enhanced costs misconduct during the course of the litigation; see Polar Ice Express Inc v Arctic Glacier Inc, 2009 ABCA 20 at paras 21–22, 446 AR 295. She found such misconduct “in the findings of credibility” made with respect to various of the [appellants], notwithstanding that she then proceeded to give specific reasons for each enhancement which did not rest on this finding of misconduct. 103 No authority precludes an award of enhanced costs because punitive damages were also awarded in the proper case. Judges have, in some cases, declined to make such an award upon concluding that remedies given, including punitive damages, were sufficient to account for the wrongdoing of the unsuccessful party. The trial judge implicitly concluded otherwise, from her comments relating to her findings of litigation misconduct. 104 Similarly, while some judges have declined to find litigation misconduct simply because of credibility findings made against certain witnesses, no authority precludes the award for that reason. In any event, the nature and depth of the negative credibility findings made against the appellants' witnesses elevates this case from the more typical situation where a trial judge simply accepts the evidence of one witness over that of others. For example, the appellants produced 11 separate affidavits of records. There was evidence that preparation for questioning took an inordinate amount of time because the transgressions could be uncovered only through detailed examination of these records, encompassing between 15,000 to 20,000 pages of documents produced by the appellants. 105 The enhanced costs award would have been justified here simply on the basis of the complexity and duration of the ligation, without reference to litigation misconduct. That practice is often followed by a judge electing to give a multiple of the appropriate column in Schedule C to reflect atypical or extraordinary aspects in the procedure leading up to judgment in a given matter. This consideration more than offsets any concern of double-compensation arising from the award of punitive damages for pre-litigation conduct. 106 The trial judge's award of enhanced costs lay well within her properly exercised discretion; see Court of Queen's Bench Act, RSA 2000, c C-31, s 21. 18. Adjournments I assume that when the bar decided to adopt the amounts set out in item 25 of the tariff, it had in mind that these are the costs that would be awarded, except in exceptional circumstances… … It is only where the parties make out a special case for additional costs that an amount other than the tariff amount should be awarded. It may well be appropriate to take into account “fault”in relation to the need for an adjournment in determining if something other than the tariff item should be applied. For example, if the party whose action necessitated the adjournment was somehow “at fault”, it may be entirely appropriate to award thrown away costs, or even punitive costs. However, where there is no “fault”, and there are no exceptional circumstances the tariff should apply. Lines v. Brink (1994), 24 Alta. L.R. (3d) 227 (Q.B.), at 238–39, per Veit J. 19. Compassion is Not a Factor In P. (S.F.) v. MacDonald (1999), 242 A.R. 134 (Q.B.), an unsuccessful plaintiff sought relief from the provisions of R 605(5). At p. 142, Veit J. said: The plaintiff asks for the court's compassion. However, the adoption of the plaintiff's argument would result in a deprivation perpetrated on the defendants. It is inappropriate, therefore, to say that compassion is an appropriate factor. It seems to me, rather, that fairness and equity are the benchmarks here. By those standards, it is fair to apply the provisions of rule 605(5) which provisions were known to the plaintiff before she opened the trial. 20. Costs in Estate Litigation In Chabros v. Anderson, 2012 ABQB 517, 2012 CarswellAlta 1422, 79 E.T.R. (3d) 317, Justice Clark considered Rules 10.33(1) and (2). He said, at paragraphs 6–15: 6 These are the rules which govern in, for lack of better term, “ordinary” civil litigation. However, both parties pointed out that costs are treated differently in estate litigation. The Executors referred to the “historical” and “modern” approaches to costs in estate litigation. 7 Historically, it was common practice in estate matters for courts to award costs of all parties out of the estate. This approach, however, has been out of favour for several years. As noted by Graesser J. of this Court in Re Foote Estate, 2010 ABQB 197 at para. 16, the “modern” approach to costs in estate litigation “requires careful scrutiny of the litigation to restrict unwarranted litigation and protect estates from being depleted by such litigation.” In more recent years, the courts have recognized that awards of costs operate to the detriment of estate beneficiaries. See, inter alia, Babchuk v. Kutz, 2007 ABQB 88 and my own reasons in Johnson v. Beers, 1999 ABQB 723, 252 AR 187. Thus, the general approach now in estate litigation is that costs follow the event unless the challenge to the will was reasonable or an exception can be justified on public policy grounds. 8 Of course, this case did not concern a challenge to the validity of the Will or proceedings to determine its proper construction. Rather, the points at issue are the proper compensation payable to the Executors for their administration of the Estate and, as a related matter, the Executors' right to be indemnified for expenses reasonably and properly incurred in the course of administration. The Executors rely upon this statement from Jennifer J. Jenkins, Compensation & Duties of Estate Trustees, Guardians & Attorneys (Toronto: Canada Law Book, 2011) at para. 22:20.20: It should be appreciated that any discussion contrasting the traditional approach to costs with the developing mindset is too simple an analysis. The issue of costs has its own particular slant, depending on the type of litigation, which hinges primarily on the role of the estate trustee. For example, a contested passing of accounts is considered to be a significant part of the administration of an estate. Thus an estate trustee is entitled to take an adversarial position in defence of his or her administration and claim for compensation and, generally speaking, the starting point is that the estate trustee and the beneficiaries are awarded costs as a legitimate expense of the estate. 9 The Executors also referred to the following comments from Donald J. (as he then was) in Re Kanee Estate (1991) 41 ETR 263 (BCSC) at paras. 17, 23, 24 and 26: There is much force in the argument advanced by Mr. Wilson that when remuneration is the only issue, the executors are acting in their own self-interest and not for the benefit of the estate and, therefore, they and any contending parties should be treated as ordinary litigants as far as costs are concerned. He endeavours to support this proposition by a decision of the Saskatchewan Surrogate Court in Re Preboy Estate (1989), 72 Sask. R. 33 (Surr. Ct.), aff'd (1989), 74 Sask. R. 223 (C.A.), where at p. 43 [72 Sask. R.] McLellan J. said: There can be no justification for the solicitors charging the beneficiaries a fee to research the law to find out what they and the executors are entitled to charge the estate. … The litigation model does not, in my opinion, fit the circumstances of this case. Executors do not step outside the estate to deal with the question of remuneration; the subject is customarily dealt with as part of the passing-of-accounts process. This is so because of the intimate connection it has with the estate. I cannot agree with Re Preboy, supra, if it purports to lay down a statement of general principle. The Court in that case did not elaborate any reasons for the statement quoted above. It is inapplicable to the case at Bar because, as the Master rightly held, it is inappropriate to set up an adversity in interest between the estate and the executors in the settlement of remuneration. Subject to considerations of reasonableness and honesty, the question of costs should be dealt with in the same way for remuneration as for the other aspects in the passing of accounts. Executors are entitled to be paid for their work. … The questioning of remuneration should not be considered in any way analogous to such truly litigious matters as claims of fraud or breach of fiduciary duty. In most cases, it will be reasonable for executors to take legal advice on remuneration and retain counsel for the passing of accounts. Since the estate owes it to the executors that they be properly remunerated, the executors, subject to just exceptions, should be fully indemnified for their costs incidental to realizing that right. 10 The Executors point out that the reasoning in Kanee was accepted by the Court in Re Wattersworth Estate 1995 CarswellOnt 2528 (Ont Ct J (Gen Div) at para. 38: Notwithstanding the authority of Widdifield on Executor's Accounts, I cannot accept as truly reflective of the law that the time spent by an estate solicitor responding to executor's questions concerning compensation allowed by law to them is not an allowable estate expense. [p.115-5th Edition (1967)] It is clearly in the estate's best interests that legitimate compensation be paid (certainly no more than what would be allowed in normal circumstances). I also happen to agree with the rationale followed by the presiding judge in [Kanee]… 11 It is not clear to me, however, that the approach in Kanee has been universally accepted. Both Kanee and Preboy have been cited in subsequent years, though largely without much analysis. 12 Moreover, as Mr. Anderson points out, Donald J. also stated in Kanee at para. 27 that “There will be cases where the executor's claim is outrageous or tainted by serious misconduct, and the discretion as to costs should be exercised differently.” Further, while the disagreement between Kanee and Preboy is noted, the following statement nevertheless appears in Carmen S. Theriault, ed., Widdifield on Executors and Trustees, 6th ed., loose-leaf (consulted on 3 July 2012) (Toronto: Thomson Canada Limited) ch. 4 at 4–21: Advice to an executor as to his right to compensation is for the personal benefit of the executor, and fees incurred to obtain the advice should not be charged against the estate. 13 Therefore, I do not think it can be said with certainty that executors are entitled to payment from the estate of legal fees incurred in respect of the determination of their appropriate compensation. Rather, I think the matter falls to be determined in accordance with the general rule that executors are entitled to be indemnified from the estate for expenses, including legal fees, reasonably and properly incurred by them in the course of their administration of that estate. I stress the words “reasonably and properly” because of the unique nature of the relationship between estate solicitors, executors and beneficiaries. In this respect, this comment from Preboy is apt: The solicitor is the solicitor for the executor, not the estate. Fees that he may charge the executor are only recoverable by the executor from the estate if it is shown that they are necessary and proper charges against the estate. 14 Similarly, the following statement appears in Widdifield at p. 4–8.3: Absent prior court approval or consent of all the beneficiaries, paying litigation accounts incurred in defending an action brought by one of the beneficiaries is not permitted. The law firm took the position that the estate was the client. The estate is not able to hire a lawyer. Until legal accounts are approved by either the court or the beneficiaries, the legal accounts are the sole responsibility of the estate trustee. The estate trustee had to reimburse the estate for the accounts that were paid, plus interest: Coppel v. Coppel Estate, [2001] O.J. No. 5246, 2001 CarswellOnt 4460 (Ont.S.C.J.) 15 It is clear, then, that executors are not entitled to assume that their legal fees will be reimbursed by the estate, regardless of circumstances or quantum. If an executor wishes to seek out “gold-plated” legal representation and/or to retain counsel to do work not necessarily required by the estate, he may do so, but he may expect to be indemnified only for the portion of that cost reasonably required for the administration of the estate. 21. Costs in Dependants Relief Act actions In Lafleur v. Lafleur, 2015 ABQB 644, Justice Greckol gave this summary of the law: 19 The Dependants Relief Act does not specify how costs should be awarded. Legislative guidance is provided by the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, rr 10.28–10.34. 20 The traditional English rule held that successful and unsuccessful parties to estate litigation could routinely recoup their costs from the estate on a substantial indemnity basis. However, appellate courts in Canada have questioned this traditional rule, suggesting there is insufficient principled reason to adhere to a special rule that conflicts directly with the conventional civil litigation costs rules. 21 Drawing from various authorities, Graesser J summarized the current principles of costs in estate litigation (Re Foote Estate, 2010 ABQB 197 at para 16, 484 AR 188): 1. The Court has a discretion with respect to costs, but that discretion must be exercised judicially; 2. The “modern” approach to costs in estate litigation requires careful scrutiny of the litigation to restrict unwarranted litigation and protect estates from being depleted by such litigation; 3. Payment of an unsuccessful party's costs out of the estate requires analysis of a number of factors: a. Did the testator cause the litigation? b. Was the challenge reasonable? c. Was the conduct of the parties reasonable? d. Was there an allegation of undue influence? e. Were there different issues or periods of time in which costs should differ? f. Were there offers to settle?; 4. There is a residual discretion where factors such as who initiated the proceedings, and the size of the estate may be relevant; 5. Costs for a successful claimant in family relief claims are generally awarded on a solicitor and client basis; 6. Costs in favour of an unsuccessful family relief claimant are an exception to the basic rule that costs follow the event; 7. Estate litigation is no longer treated as an exception to the basic rule that costs follow the event; 8. Costs will normally follow the event in estate litigation, unless the challenge to the estate was reasonable, or on the basis of a public policy exception recognizing society's interest in only probating valid wills. 22 This modern approach is a restatement of the conventional costs rule, with certain exceptions, including dependants relief litigation (St Onge Estate v Breau, 2009 NBCA 36 at para 62, 345 NBR (2d) 101 (“St Onge Estate”)). 23 Considering the sixth Foote point, one commentator stated that it is very seldom in dependants' relief litigation that courts decline to grant an unsuccessful applicant costs payable from the estate (Brian A Schnurr, Estate Litigation, vol 2, 2nd ed (Toronto: Carswell, 1994) (loose-leaf revision 5) at 19–19). This is because dependants' relief legislation is remedial, passed for social policy purposes. 24 As summarized in a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal, “[w]here the difficulties or ambiguities that give rise to the litigation are caused, in whole or in part, by the testator,” costs of all parties will be paid out of the estate (McDougald Estate v Gooderham (2005), 17 ETR (3d) 36 at para 78). Courts have characterized dependants' relief claims as those caused by the testator, and accordingly those where the unsuccessful litigant is more likely to obtain partial or full indemnification from the estate (Re Foote Estate at para 24; St Onge Estate at para 70). 25 Where costs are payable in dependants relief litigation, courts commonly order solicitor-client costs to all parties payable from the estate (Re Boje Estate, 2005 ABCA 73 at para 34, 363 AR 288; D (VT) (Next Friend of) v Spinelli Estate, 1998 ABQB 966, 229 AR 137; Stone (Public Trustee of) v Stone Estate (1994), 154 AR 307 (Alta QB)).

commentary.text:
The court may make any costs order that is appropriate in the circumstances. Ernst v. EnCana Corp. Court of , [2014] A.J. No. 1259, 2014 ABQB 672 at para. 98 (Alta. Q.B.); King’s Bench Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. C-31, s. 21. This is a wide discretion, but must be exercised judicially and in accordance with established principles. Guidance is provided in rules 10.29, 10.31, 10.33.228 Rule 10.33 addresses the considerations that go into the amount of a costs award McAllister v. Calgary (City), [2021] A.J. No. 109, 2021 ABCA 25 at para. 23 (Alta. C.A.). and, in some cases, that may guide awarding or denying costs. These factors are relevant in determining the scale of costs (party and party or enhanced costs) and, where party and party costs, may affect either the percentage of legal costs to be recovered McAllister v. Calgary (City), [2021] A.J. No. 109, 2021 ABCA 25 at paras. 45, 51 (Alta. C.A.). or the type of Schedule C calculation. Sutherland v. Sutherland Stewart , [2023] A.J. information_notes.text:
The Court has complete discretion over what to order in a costs award unless a specific rule
limits that discretion.
The typical starting point will be to decide what are the reasonable and proper costs incurred
in carrying on litigation: see rule 10.31 [Court-ordered costs award]. Rule 10.33(1) [Court
considerations in making a costs award] sets out a list of matters the Court may consider
related to the litigation (degree of success, amount involved, complexity and so on) and under
subrule (2) the Court may consider matters related to the conduct of the parties, including
unnecessary steps or delay, misconduct, and contravention of the rules or contravention of
Court orders. If the conduct of a party is found to be inappropriate, the Court can impose,
deny or vary an amount that otherwise would have been allowed in the costs award.
Note that some rules have immediate costs consequences; for example, rule 5.12 [Penalty
for not serving affidavit of records] contains a specific sanction for not serving an affidavit of
records in accordance with the rules.
